         1                      SENATOR LACK:  Thank you.

         2                      Madam President, this would

         3       extend the current authority for cameras in the

         6                      SENATOR CONNOR:  Thank you, Madam

         7       President.

         8                      In past years -- in past years,

         9       this bill has come before us.  I remember the

        10       first time it came before us when Senator

        11       Anderson brought it out under his sponsorship,

        12       and there was a big debate on the floor, and I

        13       led the debate against the then version of the

        14       bill, and it was defeated on the floor and in

        15       subsequent years it's been renewed.  It was

        16       allowed to expire.

        17                      I've voiced my opposition to this

        18       bill, but I have had an opportunity now to

        19       observe the cameras in the courtroom in action,

        20       to review a report that, while not perfect, is

        21       finally an evaluation.  I think the first

        22       experimental bill round, we all felt and many of

         1       was not truly a good view of how the experiment

         2       had worked.

         3                      So basically, in view of where we

         4       are today, Senator, I do intend to support this

         5       bill, although, of course, it is one of those

         6       bills on which members have diverse opinions and

         7       it is a matter of conscience, but I just wanted

         9                      Senator Hoffmann?

         1       waive the reading of the amendment and explain

         6                      SENATOR HOFFMANN:  Thank you.

         7                      The amendment at the desk would

         8       provide several changes in the bill, and I would

         9       like to just say at the outset that over the

        10       last decade the issue of cameras in the

        11       courtroom has gone through a very interesting

        12       evolution in New York State, and I've watched

        13       with -- with some pleasure the degree of

        14       interest that has been put forth in this house

        15       to some areas which a decade ago were not really

        16       very well considered at all, and I want to

        17       compliment the sponsor for having addressed some

        18       of the concerns that I had raised initially back

        19       in 1986 and felt like a rather lonely voice, but

        20       at that time the bill was put aside and because

        21       of the lack of unanimity on its concept, the

        22       lack of concern -- lack of unanimity on its

        23       evaluation component, we didn't have a bill at a











                                                              508

         1       point in time when there was an expectation that

         2       it would go through with very little discussion

         3       at all.

         4                      So it's one area where the

         5       involvement of this legislative body in earnest

         6       discussions, has made a difference and, while we

         7       may not find a final solution today, I hope we

         8       will come a little closer to a meeting of the

         9       minds about what is really important when we

        10       address the issue of cameras in the courtroom.

        11                      Is the paramount issue here the

        12       public's right to know, or is the paramount

        13       issue the practice of justice in New York State?

        14       And I would submit that we must still remain

        15       absolutely dedicated to the practice of justice

        16       as our number one goal and concern and recognize

        17       that a second constitutional right in this

        18       country, namely, the public's right to know, is

        19       already guaranteed.  The free press and the free

        20       trial provisions are more than adequately

        21       recognized by the open courtrooms that we have

        22       in this state.  Any of us are quite capable of

        23       going and sitting and listening to a trial.











                                                              509

         1                      We're also able to read the

         2       newspaper accounts.  But simply because we now

         3       have electronic news media as a fact of life in

         4       our homes and our bars and restaurants and

         5       legislative halls, does not mean that everything

         6       that happens in a courtroom must be or should be

         7       televised.

         8                      There are three distinct

         9       provisions within this amendment that would

        10       alter, not significantly, but would alter the

        11       bill that Senator Lack has introduced today.

        12                      One would make it very clear that

        13       a crime victim in a sex crime would have

        14       absolute veto power over cameras in the

        15       courtroom if that is the choice of that crime

        16       victim.

        17                      Another one would require that

        18       the review committee would have a representative

        19       from the Crime Victims Board so that, when we go

        20       back at the end of this evaluation period, we

        21       will have the benefit of people who are familiar

        22       with crime victims, in analyzing whether or not

        23       it has been a sensibly drawn bill and it has











                                                              510

         1       been well planned and executed in this addition

         2       al, I guess, third or fourth trial period.

         3                      And finally, and I wonder why

         4       this has to be written in at all, but yet -- and

         5       yet it does -- and finally, the amendment would

         6       include that there would be videotape repository

         7        -- a videotape repository available where all

         8       of the videotapes could be placed -- would be

         9       evaluated through the review process and would

        10       obviously be available then for the public for

        11       any further scholarly study as well as by the

        12       Legislature in ascertaining whether or not the

        13       experiment has been well conducted.

        14                      Now, why do we want these three

        15       provisions in? There is very clear anecdotal

        16       evidence, and some scattered scientific evidence

        17       to indicate that rape victims are reluctant to

        18       prosecute crimes and are most reluctant to go

        19       into a courtroom to see their attacker

        20       prosecuted if they fear there is even the

        21       slightest possibility that their own identity

        22       would be disclosed.

        23                      We have to recognize our











                                                              511

         1       responsibility here to the victims of those

         2       crimes and not put rape victims and child

         3       victims of sex crimes through any additional

         4       horror.  We should give them the right to say,

         5       "No, I do not want this trial televised."

         6       There are examples where testimony has taken

         7       place and simply inadvertently the victim's

         8       identity has been broadcast, or enough

         9       information about the victim through her place

        10       of residence, her attire, the circumstances

        11       under which the attack took place, to make it

        12       extremely evident to people who she knows,

        13       people with whom she works, other people who are

        14       simply aware of who she is, that she, in fact,

        15       was a victim of a crime.

        16                      This is another abuse heaped upon

        17       an already suffering individual, and we should

        18       allow any woman in New York State the right to

        19       say, "No, I do not want cameras in the courtroom

        20       for this trial."

        21                      Now, if she has that right, what

        22       would happen next?  All trials involving sex

        23       crimes would be closed to cameras?  No, not











                                                              512

         1       necessarily.  It would mean then that the ball

         2       is actually in the victim's court, and she would

         3       have some validity through her attorney to

         4       negotiate the circumstances under which the

         5       camera would be in the court, not be told that

         6       she would be protected by the presence of the

         7       blue dot on the screen because, as we all know,

         8       that blue dot does not always offer adequate

         9       protection.  She would then know through her

        10       attorney under which circumstances the cameras

        11       could be in the courtroom.  Possibly for some of

        12       the time, possibly for none of the time,

        13       possibly with a narrowly trained camera so that

        14       none of the courtroom would be panned because

        15       she did not want the presence of her friends and

        16       relatives panned in the courtroom to trigger

        17       what her identity is; but at the present time

        18       there is no guarantee for the victim of a rape

        19       crime that any of those conditions will be met.

        20                      The only guarantee, the only

        21       protection she has under the current measure is

        22       that her permanent identity would be protected.

        23       Inadvertent exposure, trivial aspects of her











                                                              513

         1       life, miscellaneous aspects of testimony which

         2       could lead to further humiliation are completely

         3       beyond her control and are sufficient reason for

         4       women in this state to say, "No, I will not

         5       prosecute my attacker.  I would rather let him

         6       go free, commit similar rapes against other

         7       women and children in this state rather than

         8       endure any more humiliation myself."

         9                      In the interest of justice to

        10       every rape victim in this state, we owe the

        11       right to the absolute guarantee that there will

        12       be no cameras or cameras only in a manner that

        13       are acceptable to her and in the greater

        14       interest of justice in prosecuting rapists by

        15       allowing such women to feel comfortable or at

        16       least to feel some measure of comfort in a

        17       courtroom, we should further consider the

        18       importance of this particular issue.

        19                      Judicial discretion, that's the

        20       standard phrase that's used.  The initial bill

        21       that came up in 1986 was -- was very bold and

        22       said that the judge would have judicial

        23       discretion to decide when in other circumstances











                                                              514

         1       the cameras should be taken out of the

         2       courtroom; but the phrase "judicial discretion"

         3       has come to be a very hollow one to many women

         4       who have been exposed to something lacking in

         5       discretion on the part of many judges.

         6                      We've all seen those well

         7       publicized cases where one judge, not in this

         8       state, told the -- told the public and told the

         9       jury that the -- that the victim deserved the

        10       attack because she was dressed provocatively or

        11       appeared in a provocative manner.  The victim

        12       was a minor child in that particular national

        13       scandal.  Judicial discretion was not very

        14       comforting in that instance.

        15                      There have been other cases where

        16       judges have provided comic relief at the expense

        17       of the victim, made inappropriate comments about

        18       the victim's previous sexual activities, all of

        19       which are supposedly not to be allowed in a

        20       court of law, but occasionally will happen and

        21       there is very often little sanction readily

        22       available and any abuse that takes place at the

        23       expense of the victim, if it's addressed at any











                                                              515

         1       point in the future, will not obviate the need

         2       for some remedial action right at that moment.

         3                      There is no provision in this

         4       bill to deal with the kind of inadvertent

         5       exposure of the victim's identity which could

         6       occur and, in fact, has occurred.  We had an

         7       example in New York State out in Amherst, New

         8       York during an arraignment, even while this last

         9       provision was in effect, the last trial period.

        10       We were supposed to have a guarantee that there

        11       would be no disclosure of any rape victims'

        12       names.  A victim's name and address was

        13       broadcast on the 6:00 o'clock news during an

        14       arraignment.

        15                      There's an assumption made that

        16       the broadcast industry will police itself and

        17       will follow these provisions carefully.  I don't

        18       know why people would make that assumption,

        19       because the nature of broadcasting does not

        20       include in it a -- a daily ethic course for

        21       cameramen.  It does not include in it any kind

        22       of a procedure in which every piece of videotape

        23       that is going to be shown in the 6:00 o'clock











                                                              516

         1       news in every jurisdiction in the United States

         2       or in New York State is going to be subject to

         3       careful evaluation by anybody to see whether

         4       it's complying with the standards of the test

         5       measure.

         6                      In fact, there are no sanctions

         7       against the broadcasting industry on the whole

         8       or in any individual broadcast outlet should

         9       they violate the provisions of this bill.  If

        10       they make a mistake, if they violate the privacy

        11       of a rape victim, there is no penalty for them.

        12       The only penalty available is the penalty we

        13       hold in our hands today by refusing to continue

        14       the experiment, and yet it appears that there

        15       are more than enough legislators in this state

        16       who are willing to continue the experiment for

        17       another two years.

        18                      But recognizing that the

        19       experiment has not been a one hundred percent

        20       success for the victims of sex crimes, can't we

        21       continue the experiment by allowing them the

        22       right to have cameras excluded if, in fact, that

        23       is what they desire?  And don't we have a











                                                              517

         1       responsibility to insist that, at the very

         2       least, a member of the sex crime board be

         3       included in the evaluation procedure to give all

         4       victims of sex crimes an opportunity to have

         5       their concerns addressed before we make this a

         6       permanent measure as it may some day become?

         7                      And finally, don't we have a

         8       responsibility to all of the above individuals

         9       and to ourselves as legislators, to insist that

        10       we not have only printed reports but that we

        11       maintain the actual videotape.  We are, after

        12       all, talking about broadcasting.  Isn't it a

        13       little bit ironic to have only a printed report

        14       evaluating a broadcast experiment?  Don't we

        15       have an obligation to keep in a most scientific

        16       manner the actual form of the -- of the

        17       broadcast experiment that was used so that it

        18       can then be evaluated objectively either by us

        19       or by other people who have an interest in

        20       seeing whether it continues or does not

        21       continue?

        22                      So for all of these reasons, my

        23       friends, I would ask you to consider the











                                                              518

         1       importance of this amendment and ask whether we

         2       would want to ever have to explain why, in the

         3       interest of broadcast access, any of us allowed

         4       a rape victim in this state to be subjected to

         5       greater humiliation than was absolutely

         6       necessary by permitting cameras in a courtroom

         7       over her objections.

         8                      I will continue to support the

         9       concept of cameras in the courtroom.  I'm aware

        10       of the -- the ridicule that some of us have

        11       faced through the broadcast and the print media,

        12       they're allies in opposing the greater measure

        13       of cameras in the courtroom.  I believe that

        14       cameras have a place in the courtroom in New

        15       York State.  I would like to be able to support

        16       a cameras in the courtroom bill that will

        17       address the needs of all people in New York

        18       State, but I can not support this bill unless we

        19       can pass the amendment that I presented to the

        20       desk today.

        21                      Thank you, Madam President.

        22                      THE PRESIDENT:  Thank you,

        23       Senator Hoffmann.











                                                              519

         1                      Senator Lack on the amendment.

         2                      SENATOR LACK:  Thank you, Madam

         3       President.

         4                      Senator Hoffmann, I assume you

         5       have good intentions, but the way your amendment

         6       is worded right now, it says "provided, how

         7       ever," and then it goes on and it only applies

         8       to a victim who is testifying in the case.  This

         9       is your wording, so it doesn't apply in those

        10       cases where a victim wouldn't be testifying.

        11                      As such, quite frankly, I refer

        12       you to Section 218, 7. (g) of the Judiciary Law

        13       which says:  "No audio-visual coverage shall be

        14       permitted of the victim in a prosecution for

        15       rape, sodomy, sexual abuse or other sex offense

        16       under article one hundred thirty or section

        17       255.25 of the Penal Law."  There's then a semi

        18       colon that's following that.  That's limiting,

        19       not required.  No coverage is allowed, period,

        20       even if coverage for anything else has been

        21       given.  Yes, the judge can then throw it all

        22       out.  There's no blue dot involved; there's no

        23       anything else.  When a victim of a sex crime is











                                                              520

         1       testifying at a trial, there is no coverage in

         2       New York State, period, under existing law.  No

         3       amendments to it are necessary.

         4                      As to why victims might want to

         5        -- quite frankly, we had a memorandum from

         6       Justice for All, a group of victims that

         7       supports victims having the choice if they so

         8       choose, for whatever reason a victim might want

         9       to choose to allow those proceedings to be

        10       televised; and there are victims, those who are

        11       part of Justice for All, who submitted this

        12       memorandum, who want proceedings or at least

        13       want the option to have proceedings televised as

        14       long as there's an option for the victim not to,

        15       and that's what this is all about.

        16                      So to put in an absolute

        17       prohibition, quite frankly, runs counter in some

        18       cases to some victims wanting the ability for

        19       whatever reason, they want to have it publicized

        20       what happened to them, and to want that on

        21       television.  Now, that is just as much their

        22       right, quite frankly, as is the -- as is the

        23       prohibition.











                                                              521

         1                      As to the rest of your

         2       amendments, obviously any videotapes that were a

         3       part of a report, there is a -- already a duty

         4       in law that that which goes into a report which

         5       is filed with us, particularly a committee that

         6       is formed by the chief judge of the state of New

         7       York, they're going to keep their exhibits.  We

         8       really don't have to tell the chief judge to

         9       make sure her appointees keep exhibits of

        10       audio-visual materials they've used to evaluate

        11       whatever we're requiring them to file with us,

        12       and I think it would be a little presumptuous

        13       for us to try to give that kind of instruction

        14       to the chief judge.  She knows far better than
